argument: Machiavelli argued that virtue is not a single fixed template but depends on the goal being pursued, and that a ruler's overriding goal must be the stability of the state -- without which no plan for prosperity can succeed. This justifies using force, deception, and even cruelty when necessary, since a prince must act as both fox (to recognize traps) and lion (to frighten wolves); yet Machiavelli also praised Rome's republic, resolving the apparent contradiction by treating forceful rule and republican government as two sequential stages, where stability secured by force must come before a republic can safely develop.
keyIdeas: Reducing Machiavelli to the popular sense of 'Machiavellian' misses his broader body of work, much as judging George Orwell only by Animal Farm would.

Right and wrong action depends on the goal being pursued -- what makes a good comedian differs from what makes a good doctor -- so a ruler's virtue is judged against the goal of maintaining a stable state, not the same template that applies to ordinary citizens.

A ruler's ten-year plan for prosperity is worthless without stability first, since instability undermines any progress no matter how good the plan; as Machiavelli's line about armed prophets being victorious and unarmed prophets being destroyed suggests, a new order will always face resistance from those invested in the old one.

The Prince's endorsement of an amoral, forceful ruler and the Discourses on Livy's praise of Rome's republic are reconciled as two stages of one process: a forceful ruler must first secure stability before a republic can safely develop.

Machiavelli argued a few decisive executions can be more merciful than excessive tenderness, since unchecked disorder harms the whole community while a prince's executions harm only isolated individuals -- and since love and fear rarely coexist, it is safer for a ruler to be feared than loved.

terms.def: Machiavelli's most famous work, a handbook for a new ruler on how to seize and maintain stability of a state, even through amoral means.
Machiavelli's work praising Rome's republic, drawing on the historian Livy's account of Roman government.
The chief goal Machiavelli assigns to a ruler, without which no other plan for the state can succeed.
Machiavelli's phrase for reformers who back a new order with force and thus succeed, contrasted with 'unarmed prophets' who rely on persuasion alone and are destroyed.
Machiavelli's image for the two tools a ruler needs: the fox's cunning to recognize traps (deception), and the lion's strength to frighten wolves (open threats).
